{{Short description|Formula in graph theory}}
In [[graph theory]], a '''deletion-contraction formula / recursion''' is any formula of the following [[Recurrence relation|recursive]] form:

:<math>f(G) = f(G \setminus e) + f(G / e).</math>

Here ''G'' is a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]], ''f'' is a function on graphs, ''e'' is any edge of ''G'', ''G''&nbsp;\&nbsp;''e'' denotes edge deletion, and ''G''&nbsp;/&nbsp;''e'' denotes [[Edge contraction|contraction]]. Tutte refers to such a function as a '''W-function'''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Tutte|first=W.T.|date=January 2004|title=Graph-polynomials|journal=Advances in Applied Mathematics|volume=32|issue=1–2|pages=5–9|doi=10.1016/S0196-8858(03)00041-1|doi-access=free}}</ref> The formula is sometimes referred to as the '''fundamental reduction theorem'''.<ref>{{harvtxt|Dong|Koh|Teo|2005}}</ref> In this article we abbreviate to '''DC'''.

[[R. M. Foster]] had already observed that the [[chromatic polynomial]] is one such function, and Tutte began to discover more, including a function ''f''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''t''(''G'') counting the number of [[spanning tree|spanning trees]] of a graph (also see [[Kirchhoff's theorem]]). It was later found that the [[flow polynomial]] is yet another; and soon Tutte discovered an entire class of functions called [[Tutte polynomial]]s (originally referred to as '''dichromates''') that satisfy DC.<ref name=":0" />

== Examples ==
===Spanning trees===
The number of spanning trees <math>t(G)</math> satisfies DC.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.math.wisc.edu/~svs/475/chromatic.pdf |title=Deletion-contraction and chromatic polynomials |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190504052332/https://www.math.wisc.edu/~svs/475/chromatic.pdf |archive-date=4 May 2019}}</ref>

'''Proof.''' <math>t(G \setminus e)</math> denotes the number of spanning trees not including ''e'', whereas <math>t(G/e)</math> the number including ''e''. To see the second, if ''T'' is a spanning tree of ''G'' then contracting ''e'' produces another spanning tree of <math>G/e</math>. Conversely, if we have a spanning tree ''T'' of <math>G/e</math>, then expanding the edge ''e'' gives two disconnected trees; adding ''e'' connects the two and gives a spanning tree of&nbsp;''G''.

===Laplacian characteristic polynomials===
By Kirchhoff's theorem, the number of spanning trees in a graph is counted by a cofactor of the [[Laplacian matrix]]. However, the Laplacian [[characteristic polynomial]] does not satisfy DC. By studying Laplacians with vertex weights, one can find a deletion-contraction relation between the scaled vertex-weighted Laplacian characteristic polynomials.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |title=Deletion-contraction for a unified Laplacian and applications|eprint=2110.13949 |last1=Aliniaeifard |first1=Farid |last2=Wang |first2=Victor |author3=Stephanie van Willigenburg |date=2021 |class=math.CO }}</ref>

===Chromatic polynomials===
The chromatic polynomial <math>\chi_G(k)</math> counting the number of ''k''-colorings of ''G'' does not satisfy DC, but a slightly modified formula (which can be made equivalent):<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\chi_G(k) = \chi_{G - e}(k) - \chi_{G / e}(k).</math>

'''Proof.''' If ''e'' = ''uv'', then a ''k''-coloring of ''G'' is the same as a ''k''-coloring of ''G''&nbsp;\&nbsp;''e'' where ''u'' and ''v'' have different colors. There are <math>\chi_{G\setminus e}(k)</math> total ''G''&nbsp;\&nbsp;''e'' colorings. We need now subtract the ones where ''u'' and ''v'' are colored the same. But such colorings correspond to the ''k''-colorings of <math>\chi_{G/e}(k)</math> where ''u'' and ''v'' are merged.

This above property can be used to show that the chromatic polynomial <math>\chi_G(k)</math> is indeed a [[polynomial]] in&nbsp;''k''. We can do this via [[Mathematical induction|induction]] on the number of edges and noting that in the base case where there are no edges, there are <math>k^{|V(G)|}</math> possible colorings (which is a polynomial in&nbsp;''k'').
